How the two screens stay in sync

Your teacher’s screen and yours are separate copies of the interface. A shared server stores the lesson state. The connection carries changes between each screen and that server.

Teacher’s browserMarks and feedback
↔
Session API + D1 databaseChecks permission · applies edits · keeps revisions
↔
Learner’s browserWriting and review

What this app uses

When a person edits, the browser sends an HTTP request. While the session is open, each browser checks roughly once per second for a newer revision. An unchanged reply is small. A changed reply contains the current learning state; the full lesson text is fetched when joining.

Teacher annotations and learner drafts are separate edits. The server applies each edit against the value it was based on. If two people change the same field, the conflicting version is kept and the interface asks which edit to use. A retry carries the same operation ID, so it cannot apply twice.

WebSocket, SSE, RPC and gRPC are different choices

TermWhat it doesWhat it still needs
HTTP + pollingSend edits as requests. Ask periodically whether anything changed.Shared state, permissions and retry handling. Latency includes the wait for the next check.
WebSocketOne persistent, bidirectional connection per browser. The server can immediately send changes.A shared room coordinator, reconnect/replay logic and persistent storage. Two sockets alone do not synchronize anything.
SSEA persistent server-to-browser event stream. Browsers usually send edits with separate HTTP requests.A way to notify each stream when the room changes, plus durable state and authorization.
RPCAn API style: call a remote operation such as addHighlight.A transport. That call could use HTTP or WebSocket; RPC does not choose it for you.
gRPCA typed RPC framework commonly using Protocol Buffers and HTTP/2 between services.Browser integration. The official gRPC-Web implementation supports unary calls and server streaming, not browser client/bidirectional streaming.

Why there is a database and no in-memory socket room

A static site can render both screens, but it has nowhere to coordinate them. A server that stores rooms only in memory loses them on restart. With several server instances, the teacher and learner may reach different instances.

This host provides Cloudflare Workers and D1 storage. Its Sites configuration does not expose Durable Objects, Cloudflare’s usual room coordinator. D1 lets separate Worker requests agree on the same state. A future WebSocket version could use one Durable Object per room and keep the same lesson and edit formats.

What happens when the connection drops

Unsent changes stay in the browser and remain included in a full-session export. The interface shows that they are pending. On reconnection, the browser retrieves server state and retries its edits. A deleted highlight stays deleted; a late practice tick does not bring it back.

“Hide teacher marks” is a display setting. The learner may already have received the marks, so this is not a secrecy or exam-security boundary. Room membership is enforced separately on the server.

Where overhead matters

Polling repeats requests even when there are no changes. WebSocket avoids repeated HTTP request headers after the connection is established, but still needs heartbeat, reconnection and message handling. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 can compress headers. JSON versus binary encoding changes payload size; it does not solve synchronization or conflicts. For two people reviewing words, correctness and recovery matter more than saving a few bytes.

Backups and access

sprachraum.lesson files contain teaching content. sprachraum.session files also contain drafts, saved phrases, teacher notes, marks, practice state, answers, selected tones and page positions. Restoring a session creates a separate notebook. Invitation tokens and account identities are excluded from exports.

A teacher invitation joins a room, but the teacher must also be allowed to open the hosted Site. Publishing the source on GitHub does not change that access policy.

Primary references: Cloudflare WebSockets, Durable Object rooms, D1 consistency, SSE, gRPC-Web.
